categories.description: Everyday science and how things work.

categories.name: Animals & Nature
categories.description: Wildlife, plants and the natural world.

categories.name: Around the World
categories.description: Landmarks, languages and traditions from every continent.

categories.name: Food Around the World
categories.description: Dishes, ingredients and where they come from.

categories.name: Sports
categories.description: Rules, records and the language of the game.

items.question: Which gas do plants take in from the air to make food?
items.explanation: Plants use carbon dioxide, water and sunlight in photosynthesis.

items.question: At sea level, at what temperature does water boil?
items.explanation: At standard sea-level pressure, pure water boils at 100 °C.

items.question: What is the chemical symbol for gold?
items.explanation: Au comes from the Latin word for gold, aurum.
items.source: Royal Society of Chemistry: Periodic Table — Gold

items.question: How many bones are in a typical adult human body?
items.explanation: Babies have more bones; many fuse together as we grow.

items.question: Which natural material is the hardest?
items.explanation: Diamond tops the Mohs hardness scale at 10.

items.question: Where in a human cell is most of its DNA kept?
items.explanation: The nucleus holds the chromosomes.

items.question: Roughly how fast does light travel in a vacuum?
items.explanation: The speed of light is about 299,792 km per second.

items.question: Which organ pumps blood around your body?
items.explanation: The heart pumps blood through the arteries and veins.

items.question: What is H₂O better known as?
items.explanation: Two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom make a water molecule.

items.question: Which vitamin does your skin make in sunlight?
items.explanation: UVB light helps the skin produce vitamin D.

items.question: Which gas makes up most of Earth's atmosphere?
items.explanation: Nitrogen makes up about 78% of dry air.

items.question: Which unit measures electrical resistance?
items.explanation: Resistance is measured in ohms, named after Georg Ohm.

items.question: Which is the largest ocean on Earth?
items.explanation: The Pacific covers about a third of Earth's surface.

items.question: What is the capital of Japan?
items.explanation: Tokyo has been Japan's capital since 1868.

items.question: Which river flows through Egypt and is one of the longest in the world?
items.explanation: The Nile flows north into the Mediterranean Sea.

items.question: How many continents are there, by the most common count?
items.explanation: Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Australia, Europe, North America and South America.

items.question: Which country has the largest area?
items.explanation: Russia spans about 17 million square kilometres.

items.question: What is the capital of Australia?
items.explanation: Canberra was purpose-built as the capital.

items.question: Which country's flag has a red maple leaf?
items.explanation: Canada adopted the maple leaf flag in 1965.

items.question: Mount Kilimanjaro is in which country?
items.explanation: It is in north-eastern Tanzania, near the Kenyan border.

items.question: Which desert stretches across Mongolia and northern China?
items.explanation: The Gobi is a cold desert in East Asia.

items.question: What is the capital of Brazil?
items.explanation: Brasília became the capital in 1960.

items.question: Which strait separates Spain from Morocco?
items.explanation: It links the Atlantic Ocean and the Mediterranean Sea.

items.question: Which is the smallest country in the world by area?
items.explanation: Vatican City covers less than half a square kilometre.

items.question: Which is the fastest land animal?
items.explanation: Cheetahs can sprint faster than 100 km/h over short distances.

items.question: How many legs does a spider have?
items.explanation: Spiders are arachnids, which have eight legs.

items.question: What is the largest animal known to have lived?
items.explanation: Blue whales can be around 30 metres long.

items.question: What do giant pandas mostly eat?
items.explanation: Bamboo makes up nearly all of a giant panda's diet.

items.question: What is a group of lions called?
items.explanation: Lions are the most social big cats and live in prides.

items.question: Which bird can fly backwards?
items.explanation: Hummingbirds can hover and fly in every direction.

items.question: Frogs belong to which group of animals?
items.explanation: Most amphibians start life in water and later live on land.

items.question: How many hearts does an octopus have?
items.explanation: Two hearts pump blood to the gills and one to the rest of the body.

items.question: Which tree grows acorns?
items.explanation: Acorns are the nuts of oak trees.

items.question: Which mammal can truly fly?
items.explanation: The others glide; bats are the only mammals capable of powered flight.

items.question: What is a baby kangaroo called?
items.explanation: A joey grows in its mother's pouch.

items.question: Roughly how long is an African elephant's pregnancy?
items.explanation: It is the longest pregnancy of any land mammal.

items.question: In which city is the Colosseum?
items.explanation: The Colosseum, finished in AD 80, held up to about 50,000 spectators.

items.question: The Sydney Opera House is in which country?
items.explanation: Its sail-like shells have stood on Sydney Harbour since 1973.

items.question: What is the currency of Japan?
items.explanation: The yen has been Japan's currency since 1871.

items.question: Which language has the most native speakers?
items.explanation: Mandarin has more native speakers than any other language; English has the most speakers overall.
items.source: Ethnologue: What are the top 200 most spoken languages?

items.question: Petra, a city carved into rose-red rock, is in which country?
items.explanation: The Nabataeans carved Petra's buildings out of sandstone cliffs.

items.question: The Christ the Redeemer statue looks over which city?
items.explanation: It stands on Corcovado mountain above Rio de Janeiro, Brazil.

items.question: Angkor Wat, the largest religious monument in the world, is in which country?
items.explanation: Angkor Wat was built in the 12th century and appears on Cambodia's flag.

items.question: The Mayan city of Chichén Itzá is in which country?
items.explanation: Chichén Itzá is on Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula.

items.question: Which country is famous for tulips and windmills, and has Amsterdam as its capital?
items.explanation: Amsterdam is the capital of the Netherlands.

items.question: The Acropolis looks over which capital city?
items.explanation: The Parthenon on the Acropolis was built in the 5th century BC.

items.question: Which city is nicknamed the Big Apple?
items.explanation: New York has been called the Big Apple since at least the 1920s.

items.question: The Louvre museum is in which city?
items.explanation: The Louvre, home of the Mona Lisa, is the world's most visited museum.

items.question: Which African country has the largest population?
items.explanation: Nigeria has more than 200 million people.

items.question: What is the official language of Brazil?
items.explanation: Brazil was a Portuguese colony until 1822.

items.question: Which country's flag is a red circle on a white background?
items.explanation: Japan's flag is the Hinomaru, the 'circle of the sun'. Bangladesh's red circle sits on green.

items.question: Neuschwanstein, the fairy-tale castle, is in which country?
items.explanation: King Ludwig II of Bavaria built it in the 19th century.

items.question: Which country is shaped like a boot?
items.explanation: Italy's peninsula looks like a boot kicking Sicily.

items.question: What is the currency of the United Kingdom?
items.explanation: The pound sterling is one of the oldest currencies still in use.

items.question: The Alhambra palace is in which Spanish city?
items.explanation: The Alhambra was built by the Nasrid rulers of Granada.

items.question: Which country has more ancient pyramids than Egypt?
items.explanation: Sudan has around 200 Nubian pyramids, more than Egypt.

items.question: Which country gave the Statue of Liberty to the United States?
items.explanation: It was a gift from the people of France, dedicated in 1886.

items.question: The haka is a traditional dance of which people?
items.explanation: New Zealand's rugby team performs a haka before matches.

items.question: Which Italian city's carnival is famous for elaborate masks?
items.explanation: Masked balls have been part of the Carnival of Venice for centuries.

items.question: Stonehenge is in which country?
items.explanation: Stonehenge stands on Salisbury Plain in southern England.

items.question: In which country is Día de los Muertos (Day of the Dead) celebrated with marigolds and sugar skulls?
items.explanation: Families honour their dead on 1 and 2 November.

items.question: In Japan, hanami is the custom of viewing which flowers?
items.explanation: Friends picnic under the blossoming sakura trees each spring.

items.question: What is another name for the Northern Lights?
items.explanation: Aurora australis is the Southern Lights.

items.question: Marrakech is a city in which country?
items.explanation: Marrakech's old town is famous for its souks and the square Jemaa el-Fna.

items.question: Lake Titicaca lies on the border between Peru and which country?
items.explanation: It is one of the highest large lakes in the world.

items.question: Which country is famous for its fjords and is home to the city of Bergen?
items.explanation: Bergen is the gateway to Norway's western fjords.

items.question: Which is the largest planet in our solar system?
items.explanation: Jupiter is more than twice as massive as all the other planets combined.

items.question: Which planet is known as the Red Planet?
items.explanation: Iron oxide dust gives Mars its reddish colour.

items.question: Which star is closest to Earth?
items.explanation: Trick question: the Sun is a star. Proxima Centauri is the next closest.

items.question: Who was the first person to walk on the Moon?
items.explanation: Armstrong stepped onto the Moon on 20 July 1969 (Apollo 11).

items.question: Which planet is famous for its bright rings?
items.explanation: Saturn's rings are mostly ice and rock.

items.question: About how long does sunlight take to reach Earth?
items.explanation: Light covers the 150 million km in roughly 8 minutes 20 seconds.

items.question: In 2014, which lander became the first spacecraft to land on a comet?
items.explanation: Philae, carried by ESA's Rosetta, landed on comet 67P.

items.question: Which planet is closest to the Sun?
items.explanation: Mercury orbits the Sun every 88 days.

items.question: What is the chemical symbol for sodium?
items.explanation: Na comes from natrium, the Latin name for sodium.
items.source: Royal Society of Chemistry: Periodic Table, sodium

items.question: In which part of a plant does most photosynthesis happen?
items.explanation: Leaves are full of chloroplasts, which capture sunlight to make food.

items.question: Which blood cells carry oxygen around the body?
items.explanation: Red blood cells contain haemoglobin, which binds oxygen.

items.question: Which force keeps the planets in orbit around the Sun?
items.explanation: The Sun’s gravity pulls on each planet and bends its path into an orbit.

items.question: Which element has the atomic number 1?
items.explanation: Hydrogen has one proton, making it the first element in the periodic table.
items.source: Royal Society of Chemistry: Periodic Table, hydrogen

items.question: What is the largest organ of the human body?
items.explanation: Skin covers the whole body and is its largest organ.

items.question: Which metal is a liquid at room temperature?
items.explanation: Mercury melts at about −39 °C, so it is liquid at room temperature.
items.source: Royal Society of Chemistry: Periodic Table, mercury

items.question: Sound travels fastest through which of these?
items.explanation: Sound moves faster through solids than liquids or gases, and not at all through a vacuum.

items.question: What is the pH of pure water at 25 °C?
items.explanation: Pure water is neutral, with a pH of 7 at 25 °C.

items.question: Which scientist described the three laws of motion?
items.explanation: Newton published his laws of motion in 1687, in the Principia.

items.question: How many chambers does the human heart have?
items.explanation: Two atria receive blood and two ventricles pump it out.

items.question: Which gas makes the bubbles in fizzy drinks?
items.explanation: Carbon dioxide is dissolved under pressure and bubbles out when the bottle is opened.

items.question: Which part of the eye changes the size of the pupil?
items.explanation: The coloured iris widens or narrows the pupil to control how much light gets in.

items.question: What is the SI unit of force?
items.explanation: One newton accelerates one kilogram by one metre per second, every second.
items.source: BIPM: The International System of Units

items.question: Which type of rock forms when lava or magma cools?
items.explanation: Igneous rocks, such as basalt and granite, form from cooled molten rock.

items.question: What is the hardest substance in the human body?
items.explanation: Enamel, the outer layer of teeth, is harder than bone.

items.question: What do we call animals that eat only plants?
items.explanation: Herbivores, like cows and deer, eat plants only.

items.question: What is the centre of an atom called?
items.explanation: The nucleus holds protons and neutrons; electrons move around it.

items.question: What is the capital of Canada?
items.explanation: Ottawa, in Ontario, is the capital; Toronto is Canada’s largest city.

items.question: Which river carries more water than any other river in the world?
items.explanation: The Amazon’s discharge is far greater than any other river’s.

items.question: Which is the largest hot desert in the world?
items.explanation: The Sahara covers much of North Africa. Only the cold polar deserts are larger.

items.question: What is the capital of Kenya?
items.explanation: Nairobi is Kenya’s capital and largest city.

items.question: Which mountain range is usually taken as the border between Europe and Asia?
items.explanation: The Urals run north to south across Russia and mark the conventional boundary.

items.question: What is the capital of Italy?
items.explanation: Rome has been Italy’s capital since 1871.

items.question: Which ocean lies between Africa and Australia?
items.explanation: The Indian Ocean is bounded by Africa, Asia and Australia.

items.question: Which is the largest island in the world, not counting continents?
items.explanation: Greenland is the world’s largest island; Australia counts as a continent.

items.question: Which US state is made up entirely of islands?
items.explanation: Hawaii is a chain of volcanic islands in the Pacific.

items.question: Along which side of South America do the Andes run?
items.explanation: The Andes run along the western, Pacific side of the continent.

items.question: What is the capital of Egypt?
items.explanation: Cairo sits on the Nile, near the head of its delta.

items.question: Which is the largest lake in Africa?
items.explanation: Lake Victoria is shared by Uganda, Kenya and Tanzania.

items.question: What is the capital of South Korea?
items.explanation: Seoul is South Korea’s capital and largest city.

items.question: What is the capital of Iceland?
items.explanation: Reykjavík is the world’s northernmost capital of a sovereign state.

items.question: Which sea lies between southern Europe and North Africa?
items.explanation: The Mediterranean is almost enclosed by Europe, Africa and Asia.

items.question: Which imaginary line divides Earth into Northern and Southern Hemispheres?
items.explanation: The Equator is the line of 0° latitude.

items.question: Angel Falls, the world’s highest uninterrupted waterfall, is in which country?
items.explanation: Angel Falls drops about 979 metres in Venezuela’s Canaima National Park.

items.question: Which country is home to Istanbul and lies partly in Europe and partly in Asia?
items.explanation: Istanbul sits on both sides of the Bosporus strait.

items.question: How many legs does an insect have?
items.explanation: All adult insects have six legs; spiders, with eight, are not insects.

items.question: What is the largest bird in the world?
items.explanation: Ostriches can stand over 2.5 metres tall. They can’t fly but run very fast.

items.question: Which animal is called the "ship of the desert"?
items.explanation: Camels can travel long distances in the desert with little water.

items.question: What do caterpillars grow into?
items.explanation: Caterpillars are the larvae of butterflies and moths.

items.question: Which part of a plant takes in water from the soil?
items.explanation: Roots absorb water and minerals and anchor the plant.

items.question: What is a group of crows called?
items.explanation: "A murder of crows" is a traditional collective noun.

items.question: Which is the largest species of shark?
items.explanation: Whale sharks are the largest living fish, and they eat plankton.

items.question: Snakes collect scents from the air using which body part?
items.explanation: The tongue carries scent particles to a sensing organ in the roof of the mouth.

items.question: Which of these animals is a marsupial?
items.explanation: Koalas carry their young in a pouch; they are not bears.

items.question: What colour is a polar bear’s skin?
items.explanation: Under the pale fur, polar bear skin is black, which helps absorb heat.

items.question: Chocolate is made from the seeds of which tree?
items.explanation: Cacao seeds, often called cocoa beans, are fermented, dried and roasted.

items.question: What do koalas mainly eat?
items.explanation: Koalas feed almost entirely on eucalyptus leaves.

items.question: Which of these mammals lays eggs?
items.explanation: The platypus is one of the few egg-laying mammals, called monotremes.

items.question: How many wings does a honeybee have?
items.explanation: Bees have two pairs of wings that hook together in flight.

items.question: Which is the tallest animal in the world?
items.explanation: Adult giraffes can be over 5 metres tall.

items.question: What do fish take out of the water with their gills?
items.explanation: Gills absorb oxygen dissolved in the water.

items.question: Which flower’s young plants turn to follow the Sun across the sky?
items.explanation: Growing sunflowers track the Sun from east to west during the day.

items.question: What is a female deer called?
items.explanation: Female deer are does (or hinds in some species); males are bucks or stags.

items.question: What is the name of our galaxy?
items.explanation: The Sun is one of hundreds of billions of stars in the Milky Way.

items.question: Which planet spins on its side, tilted about 98 degrees?
items.explanation: Uranus rolls around the Sun on its side, probably after an ancient collision.

items.question: Which is the hottest planet in our solar system?
items.explanation: Venus’s thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat, making it hotter than Mercury.

items.question: What was the first artificial satellite, launched in 1957?
items.explanation: The Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1 on 4 October 1957.

items.question: Who was the first human to travel into space?
items.explanation: Gagarin orbited Earth in Vostok 1 on 12 April 1961.

items.question: Who was the first woman to travel into space?
items.explanation: Tereshkova flew on Vostok 6 in June 1963.

items.question: Which space telescope, launched in 2021, looks at the universe mainly in infrared?
items.explanation: Webb's gold mirror is 6.5 metres across.

items.question: What does a light-year measure?
items.explanation: It is the distance light travels in one year, about 9.46 trillion km.

items.question: Which planet has the Great Red Spot, a giant storm?
items.explanation: The Great Red Spot is a storm larger than Earth.

items.question: Roughly how long does the Moon take to orbit Earth?
items.explanation: The Moon orbits Earth about every 27.3 days.

items.question: Which object was counted as the ninth planet until 2006?
items.explanation: The International Astronomical Union reclassified Pluto as a dwarf planet in 2006.

items.question: What is the boundary around a black hole, beyond which nothing can escape, called?
items.explanation: Not even light can get back out once it crosses the event horizon.

items.question: Which ancient civilisation built the pyramids at Giza?
items.explanation: They were built as royal tombs about 4,500 years ago.

items.question: In which year did the Second World War end?
items.explanation: The war ended in Europe in May 1945 and in Asia in September 1945.

items.question: Who led the first expedition to reach the South Pole, in 1911?
items.explanation: Amundsen's team arrived about a month before Scott's.

items.question: Which wall divided a European city from 1961 to 1989?
items.explanation: The Berlin Wall split East and West Berlin until it fell in 1989.

items.question: Which ship sank on its first voyage in 1912 after hitting an iceberg?
items.explanation: RMS Titanic sank in the North Atlantic on 15 April 1912.

items.question: Who painted the Mona Lisa?
items.explanation: Leonardo painted it in the early 1500s; it hangs in the Louvre.

items.question: Which empire was ruled from Constantinople for about a thousand years?
items.explanation: The Byzantine Empire lasted until Constantinople fell in 1453.

items.question: In 1893, women in which country became the first to win the vote in national elections?
items.explanation: New Zealand gave women the vote in 1893.

items.question: Whose expedition made the first voyage around the world (1519–1522)?
items.explanation: Magellan died on the way; Juan Sebastián Elcano brought the last ship home.

items.question: Vasco da Gama reached which Indian port by sea in 1498?
items.explanation: His voyage opened a sea route from Europe to India around Africa.

items.question: Which Roman city was buried when Mount Vesuvius erupted in AD 79?
items.explanation: Ash preserved Pompeii so well that it is still being excavated.

items.question: Who was the first President of the United States?
items.explanation: Washington took office in 1789.

items.question: Who developed the movable-type printing press in Europe around 1440?
items.explanation: Gutenberg’s press made books far cheaper and faster to produce.

items.question: The Terracotta Army was buried to guard the tomb of which ruler?
items.explanation: Thousands of clay soldiers guard China's first emperor.

items.question: In which country did the Industrial Revolution begin?
items.explanation: It began in Britain in the 18th century with machines powered by water and steam.

items.question: Who was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize?
items.explanation: Marie Curie shared the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics, and won Chemistry in 1911.

items.question: In which year was the Magna Carta sealed in England?
items.explanation: King John sealed it at Runnymede in 1215.

items.question: Which civilisation built Machu Picchu?
items.explanation: The Inca built it high in the Andes of Peru in the 15th century.
items.source: UNESCO: Historic Sanctuary of Machu Picchu

items.question: Who gave the "I Have a Dream" speech in 1963?
items.explanation: King spoke at the March on Washington for civil rights.

items.question: Nelson Mandela became president of which country in 1994?
items.explanation: He was South Africa’s first president elected in a fully democratic vote.

items.question: Sushi is a traditional dish from which country?
items.explanation: Sushi combines vinegared rice with fish, vegetables or seaweed.

items.question: Paella is a rice dish from which country?
items.explanation: Paella comes from the Valencia region of Spain.

items.question: Risotto is made with which grain?
items.explanation: Short-grain rice is slowly cooked in stock until creamy.

items.question: What is the main ingredient of guacamole?
items.explanation: Guacamole is mashed avocado with lime, onion and chilli.

items.question: Hummus is made mainly from which legume?
items.explanation: Chickpeas are blended with tahini, lemon and garlic.

items.question: Kimchi, a spicy fermented dish, comes from which country?
items.explanation: Kimchi is usually made from cabbage and radish.

items.question: Which spice, from a crocus flower, is the most expensive by weight?
items.explanation: Each saffron thread is a hand-picked part of the flower.

items.question: Tofu is made from which bean?
items.explanation: Soy milk is curdled and pressed into blocks.

items.question: Pad thai is a noodle dish from which country?
items.explanation: Pad thai is stir-fried rice noodles, often with peanuts and lime.

items.question: What kind of food is Parmigiano Reggiano?
items.explanation: It is a hard Italian cheese aged for at least a year.

items.question: Croissants are most associated with the bakeries of which country?
items.explanation: The flaky, buttery croissant is a staple of French breakfasts.

items.question: Traditional Mexican tortillas are made from which grain?
items.explanation: Corn is treated with lime, ground into dough and pressed flat.

items.question: Raisins are dried versions of which fruit?
items.explanation: Dried plums are prunes; dried grapes are raisins.

items.question: Marzipan is made mainly from which nut?
items.explanation: Ground almonds are mixed with sugar into a smooth paste.

items.question: Pho is a noodle soup from which country?
items.explanation: Pho is broth with rice noodles, herbs and usually beef or chicken.

items.question: Pierogi, filled dumplings, are a national dish of which country?
items.explanation: Pierogi are also popular across Central and Eastern Europe.

items.question: Couscous, made from semolina, is a staple in which region?
items.explanation: Couscous is central to Moroccan, Algerian and Tunisian cooking.

items.question: The tea ceremony called chanoyu comes from which country?
items.explanation: It is a ritual way of preparing and serving powdered green tea.

items.question: Feta cheese traditionally comes from which country?
items.explanation: Feta is made from sheep’s milk, sometimes mixed with goat’s milk.

items.question: Which country is the original home of the potato?
items.explanation: Potatoes were first farmed in the Andes of South America thousands of years ago.

items.question: How many players does a football (soccer) team have on the field?
items.explanation: Each side fields ten outfield players and a goalkeeper.
items.source: IFAB: Laws of the Game, Law 3

items.question: In which sport would you see a slam dunk?
items.explanation: A slam dunk is pushing the ball down through the hoop.

items.question: How many rings are on the Olympic flag?
items.explanation: The five rings represent the union of the world’s continents.

items.question: In tennis, what is a score of zero called?
items.explanation: A game score of 0 is called "love".

items.question: In cricket, what is it called when a batter is out without scoring?
items.explanation: A batter dismissed for zero is "out for a duck".

items.question: How long is a standard marathon?
items.explanation: The distance is 42.195 km; a half marathon is half that.

items.question: Which country hosted the first modern Olympic Games in 1896?
items.explanation: The first modern Games were held in Athens.

items.question: In chess, which piece moves only diagonally?
items.explanation: A bishop stays on squares of one colour all game.

items.question: How many squares are on a chessboard?
items.explanation: The board has eight rows of eight squares.

items.question: Which country won the first FIFA World Cup, in 1930?
items.explanation: Uruguay hosted and won, beating Argentina 4–2 in the final.

items.question: In which sport is one under par on a hole called a birdie?
items.explanation: Two under par is an eagle; one over is a bogey.

items.question: How many points is a touchdown worth in American football?
items.explanation: A touchdown is worth six points, before any extra point attempt.

items.question: What colour is the centre of a standard archery target?
items.explanation: From the centre out, the rings are gold, red, blue, black and white.

items.question: Which sport uses a shuttlecock?
items.explanation: The shuttlecock is traditionally made of feathers and cork.

items.question: The Thomas Cup is the world team championship of which sport?
items.explanation: The Thomas Cup is for men’s teams; the Uber Cup is for women’s teams.

items.question: What is the highest score possible with three darts?
items.explanation: Three darts in the treble 20 score 180.

items.question: In which sport do players form a scrum?
items.explanation: A scrum restarts play after minor infringements in rugby.

items.question: In motor racing, what does the chequered flag mean?
items.explanation: The chequered flag is waved as the winner crosses the line.

items.question: How many holes are played in a standard round of golf?
items.explanation: A full round is 18 holes; many courses also offer 9.

items.question: How many players are on the court for each team in volleyball?
items.explanation: Indoor volleyball teams have six players on court.
